blocks.text: A trader in Onitsha does not count grains of rice one by one. She weighs a bag and knows roughly how many grains are inside. Chemists face the same problem on a far bigger scale: atoms are far too small to count. The mole is the chemist's way of counting particles by weighing them.

blocks.title: The mole
blocks.text: One mole is the amount of substance that contains as many elementary particles as there are atoms in 12 g of carbon-12. That number is the Avogadro constant, 6.02 x 10 to the power 23 per mole, written as NA.

blocks.markdown:
## Molar mass

The **molar mass** of a substance is the mass of one mole of it, measured in grams per mole. Its numerical value is the same as the relative atomic mass or relative molecular mass.

- One mole of carbon atoms has a mass of 12 g
- One mole of water molecules has a mass of 18 g
- One mole of sodium chloride has a mass of 58.5 g

To find a molar mass, add the relative atomic masses of every atom in the formula. For calcium hydroxide, Ca(OH)2:

40 + 2 x (16 + 1) = 40 + 34 = 74 g/mol

blocks.caption: n = number of moles, m = mass in g, M = molar mass in g/mol, N = number of particles

items: Mass to moles: divide the mass by the molar mass
Moles to mass: multiply the number of moles by the molar mass
Moles to particles: multiply the number of moles by 6.02 x 10^23
Particles to moles: divide the number of particles by 6.02 x 10^23
Moles of gas to volume at s.t.p.: multiply the number of moles by 22.4 dm3

blocks.title: Mass to moles and then to particles
blocks.prompt: Calculate the number of moles and the number of formula units in 25 g of calcium carbonate, CaCO3. Take Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16 and NA = 6.02 x 10^23 per mole.

steps.text: First find the molar mass by adding the relative atomic masses in the formula: Ca = 40, C = 12, and three O atoms give 3 x 16 = 48.
Apply n = m / M with m = 25 g.
Now convert moles to particles using N = n x NA.
Multiply out: 0.25 x 6.02 = 1.505, so N = 1.505 x 10^23 formula units.
Check the size of the answer: a quarter of a mole should give roughly a quarter of the Avogadro constant, and 1.5 x 10^23 is indeed about a quarter of 6.02 x 10^23.

blocks.answer: 0.25 mol, containing 1.505 x 10^23 formula units of CaCO3

blocks.caption: Molar masses of substances that appear constantly in WAEC calculations

blocks.title: Moles of molecules versus moles of atoms
blocks.text: One mole of water contains 6.02 x 10^23 molecules but 3 x 6.02 x 10^23 atoms, because each molecule has two hydrogens and one oxygen. Read the question carefully: it makes a threefold difference to the answer.

blocks.title: Set out the formula every time
blocks.text: Write n = m / M, substitute the numbers with units, then evaluate. Method marks are awarded for the correct substitution even if the arithmetic slips, but an unsupported number earns nothing if it is wrong.

points: One mole contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles, the Avogadro constant.
Molar mass in g/mol is numerically equal to relative atomic or molecular mass.
Number of moles = mass divided by molar mass.
Number of particles = number of moles multiplied by the Avogadro constant.
Distinguish carefully between moles of molecules and moles of the individual atoms inside them.
